title: Unlucky Numbers Around the World (and the Stories Behind Them)
description: Why buildings in Asia skip the 4th floor, why 9 sounds like suffering in Japan, why Italians fear Friday the 17th, why 8 decided when the Beijing Olympics began, why the oldest copy of the Bible says 616 instead of 666, and why 11:11 keeps following you.

segments.text: In Mandarin, the number four sounds like the word for death.
In Japan, nine can sound like the word for suffering.
In Italy, seventeen hides a word that was carved on Roman tombs.
And in the West, plenty of people still won't live on the thirteenth floor.
Every culture has a number it avoids. And a number it chases.
Today we're going through nine of them, from the number that erases buttons in elevators, to the number that decided when an Olympic Games began.
And stay for the last one. It has probably happened to you today.
Number one. Four.
Step into an elevator in Hong Kong, Shanghai or Seoul, and there's a good chance the button for four is missing.
The reason is sound. In Mandarin, four is sì, and death is sǐ. Only the tone is different.
Japanese has the same problem. Four can be read as shi, which is also a word for death. So people often say yon instead.
In Korea, the fourth floor is often marked with the letter F, especially in hospitals.
Some buildings skip fourteen and twenty-four as well. And a few towers in Hong Kong leave out every floor in the forties.
There's even a name for it. Tetraphobia.
But four isn't the only number Japan avoids.
Number two. Nine.
In Japanese, nine can be read as ku. And ku is also the sound of a word for suffering.
That's why nine is usually spoken as kyuu, and why some hospitals and hotels avoid room numbers with a four or a nine.
Put the two together, and forty-nine can be read as shi ku. Death and suffering.
Meanwhile, in the West, nine is mostly a happy number. Cloud nine. A cat's nine lives.
Which is a good reminder. The number never changes. Only the words around it do.
And the West has its own number it would rather skip.
Number three. Thirteen.
Look at the buttons in many hotels and towers, and you'll find a twelve, and then a fourteen.
The thirteenth floor is usually still there. It just has a different name.
Two old stories sit behind the fear. At the Last Supper, thirteen sat at the table.
And in Norse myth, the trickster Loki arrived as the uninvited thirteenth guest at a feast of the gods.
Put thirteen on a Friday, and the fear even gets its own word. Paraskevidekatriaphobia.
Then there's Apollo 13. It launched at thirteen thirteen, Houston time, and an oxygen tank exploded on April the thirteenth.
All three astronauts still made it home. So maybe thirteen isn't as unlucky as its reputation.
Italy, though, never worried much about thirteen. It has its own number.
Number four. Seventeen.
Write seventeen in Roman numerals, and you get X, V, I, I.
Now move the letters around. V, I, X, I. Vixi.
In Latin, vixi means I have lived. In other words, my life is over. It was carved on Roman tombstones.
So in Italy, the unlucky day isn't Friday the thirteenth. It's Friday the seventeenth.
Some Italian airlines have even left row seventeen off their planes.
From the unluckiest number in Italy, to the luckiest number in China.
Number five. Eight.
On the eighth of August, 2008, the Beijing Olympics opened at eight in the evening.
You may have heard it started at eight oh eight. The official start was eight o'clock. But the date was no accident.
In Mandarin, eight is bā. It sounds close to fā, a word tied to wealth and prosperity.
So people pay real money for phone numbers and license plates full of eights.
Turn an eight on its side, and you get the symbol for infinity.
Which brings us to the most feared number of all. Or is it?
Number six. Six six six.
It comes from the Book of Revelation, where it's called the number of the beast.
But the oldest copy of that verse we have doesn't say six six six.
It's a papyrus fragment from Egypt, about seventeen hundred years old, known as Papyrus 115. And it says six one six.
Even in the second century, a bishop named Irenaeus knew about six one six, and argued that six six six was correct.
And here's the twist. In Chinese internet slang, six six six is a compliment.
Six is liù, which sounds like a word for smooth, or slick. Typing six six six means: that was skilful. Nicely done.
So one number can be a warning on one side of the world, and applause on the other.
Number seven. Seven.
If there's one number almost every culture likes, it's seven. And the reason might be right above your head.
Ancient sky watchers saw seven lights moving against the stars. The Sun, the Moon, Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus and Saturn.
Each one got a day of the week. Sunday, the Sun. Monday, the Moon. Saturday, Saturn.
In Spanish you can still hear the others. Martes, miércoles, jueves, viernes.
Seven days, seven lights. A week is, quite literally, a small model of the sky.
Our next number hides in plain sight, in almost every shop window.
Number eight. Ten past ten.
Look at almost any watch advertisement, and the hands point to ten past ten.
There's a popular story that it marks the moment Abraham Lincoln was shot. It's a myth.
Watchmakers give a simpler reason. At ten past ten, the hands frame the logo and never hide the small dials.
Older ads often used eight twenty. But eight twenty looks like a frown.
Ten past ten looks like a smile. And once you notice it, you'll never stop seeing it.
Which is exactly the secret of our last number.
Number nine. Eleven eleven.
You glance at the clock, and it's eleven eleven. Again.
For many people, it's a moment to make a wish. And the eleventh of November is the biggest wishing day of the year.
But that date carried weight long before angel numbers. The First World War ended at the eleventh hour of the eleventh day of the eleventh month, in 1918.
So why does eleven eleven seem to follow you? There's a name for that. The frequency illusion.
Once something matters to you, your brain starts flagging it. You never notice ten forty-eight. But every eleven eleven jumps out.
So is it just your brain? Maybe. But your brain chose to notice. And what you were thinking about at that moment might be the real message.
Four, nine, thirteen, seventeen. Eight, six six six, seven, ten past ten, and eleven eleven.
The numbers never changed. The stories around them did.
So tell me. Which number do you avoid? And which one do you chase?
There are more stories like these on this channel. I'll see you in the next one.
